model_or_family: Panther Box Fuzz-Tone and Treble Boost
evidence_summary: Tone Machines identifies the Goya Panther as the strongest hard-evidence anchor for the early Applied fuzz family. Its 1967 release timing, unusual battery-test arrangement, and construction details are used as the reference state for later Applied-related variants. This record does not claim a surviving factory contract document.

Tone Machines identifies Kadent as clearly related to the Applied fuzz platform while noting that the exact point in the Applied timeline remains uncertain. The variant has distinct early construction features and may predate the better-documented 1968 Applied ads, but the production date is not proven. Specialist discussion confirms the surviving Kadent example and early circuit variant.

Tone Machines identifies the Giulietti fuzz and treble booster as an early example of the same Applied-related product family, noting the large battery lamp and treble on/off pot seen on early examples. Effects Database documents Giulietti as a New York company that sold rebranded guitar gear and the specific fuzz/treble booster model. No period factory document was located in this pass.

Tone Machines identifies Vivant-branded examples as part of the Applied Fuzz and Treble Booster family and notes both early and later forms, including an early form with the large battery lamp and treble on/off pot. The associated distributor or brand history remains unresolved, so Vivant is not treated as a factory identity.

Tone Machines reports that the 1967-68 Applied facility history explicitly placed Sano among brands for which Applied was already building amplifiers and effects. The specific Sano fuzz is grouped with the early Applied two-in-one fuzz/treble booster family, but the exact model-level period source is not yet sufficient for promotion to high confidence.

Effects Database and Tone Machines both place the Crown fuzz and treble booster in the early Applied two-in-one platform. The Crown example is specifically discussed as an early construction state with the large battery-test lamp and treble on/off control. Exact Crown corporate identity remains unresolved, but the physical-builder relationship is well supported.

Effects Database identifies the Lou Rose Combo-Fuzz as manufactured by Applied Audio Products Inc. around 1968. Tone Machines dates the Lou Rose Music Center opening to September 1968 and reports a small initial run of units, providing a useful period anchor for the early Applied family.
